newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Americas deputy ministers discuss trade deal.
newsitem.headline: Americas deputy ministers discuss trade deal.

text.p: Deputy trade ministers from 34 countries in the Americas gathered in the Brazilian industrial city of Belo Horizonte on Tuesday to hammer out a deal on a region-wide free trade zone, officials said.

The officials said the deputy ministers will draw a declaration to be signed by their political bosses on Friday at the end of the third ministerial meeting of Free Trade Area of the Americas (FTAA) signatory countries.

Brazilian officials conceded that an accord was still beyond reach because of a dispute between the United States and the South American Mercosur trade bloc, led by Brazil, over the timetable and nature of formal negotiations.

"The United States says formal negotiations must be launched no matter what (after a presidential FTAA summit in Chile next March), which Mercosur opposes," Jose Botafogo Goncalves, general subsecretary for economic integration and international trade at the Brazilian Foreign Ministry, said late on Monday.
Launched at the Miami summit in 1994, the FTAA envisioned the setting up of a free trade area of one billion potential consumers by 2005 that would rival the economic muscle of the European Union.

Trade and foreign ministers, due to gather in Belo Horizonte on May 15-16 after the deputy ministers conclude their talks, were supposed to determine the timetable and nature of formal free trade negotiations.
But progress was blocked by disagreement between Brazil, speaking for Mercosur, and Washington.

Brazil was keen to strengthen Mercosur. But faced with a ballooning trade gap, it was uneasy over the prospect of taking on further tariff-reduction obligations that would allow entry of more imports. It urged "caution and prudence" in progress towards the FTAA.

Brazil also sought assurances from Washington that free trade will apply to all sectors, including agriculture, and President Fernando Henrique Cardoso sent a clear message to Washington on Monday that it would have to give as well as take.
The United States, on the other hand, was determined to push through free trade as fast as possible.
Parallel to the official trade talks in Belo Horizonte, hundreds of businessmen from across the region poured into the city of two million people to hold a forum starting on Wednesday.
Labour leaders from across the Americas began meeting Monday and were expected to present a list of their demands and suggestions on Tuesday to the deputy ministers.

One of the decisions the Belo Horizonte meeting was expected to make was whether to allow the labour movement greater involvement in the negotiation process by allowing it to also hold parallel forums similar to the businessmen.
Officials from Brazil and the United States said they back the proposal but other countries were said to be opposed.
